name: Area-law entanglement makes MPS and DMRG efficient
summary: The Schmidt rank across any cut of a matrix product state is at most the bond dimension, so the entanglement entropy obeys S ≤ ln χ. Ground states of gapped 1D Hamiltonians obey an area law (Hastings 2007), so they compress efficiently, and entanglement growth sets the cost of time evolution.

name: Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument
summary: The 1927–35 Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument treated completeness and locality as philosophical questions. Bell (1964) turned them into testable inequalities, which is why foundations of QM is where history and philosophy meet the laboratory.

name: The quantum revolution, 1900–1927
summary: Blackbody radiation (Planck 1900), the photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905) and atomic spectra with the Bohr model (1913) led to matrix and wave mechanics (1925–26). Spectroscopy drove the experiments, and the episode is the standard case study of theory change.

name: Measurement problem and rival interpretations
summary: Unitary evolution and definite measurement outcomes conflict. Copenhagen, Everett's relative states, Bohmian mechanics, GRW collapse and QBism resolve this in different ways, and the meaning of Born-rule probability in many worlds is debated in both fields.

name: Eigenproblems and special functions of quantum mechanics
summary: Separation of variables, Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems and orthogonal polynomials (Hermite, Laguerre, Legendre) give the textbook spectra. Green's functions, contour integrals and asymptotic methods underpin perturbation theory, scattering and WKB.

name: Spectral theorem as the measurement postulate
summary: States are rays in a Hilbert space and observables are self-adjoint operators. The spectral theorem supplies the possible outcomes (eigenvalues) and projectors that give the Born rule and state update. Gleason's theorem shows this is the only consistent probability measure for dimension ≥ 3.

name: Rotation symmetry labels states and selection rules
summary: Rotational invariance of H makes j and m good quantum numbers. The Wigner–Eckart theorem splits every tensor-operator matrix element into a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient times a reduced element, which gives the dipole selection rules.

name: Spin is a projective representation of SO(3)
summary: Angular-momentum operators obey the su(2) algebra, whose irreducible representations give j = 0, 1/2, 1, …. Half-integer spin exists because SU(2) double-covers SO(3): a 2π rotation multiplies a spinor by −1, as seen in neutron interferometry.

name: The SI second is a caesium hyperfine frequency
summary: Since 1967 the second has been defined by fixing the Cs ground-state hyperfine frequency. Time and frequency are the most precisely realised SI quantities, and the metre is traced to them through the fixed value of c.

name: AMO measurements determine α and m_e for CODATA
summary: The fine-structure constant comes from atom-recoil interferometry (h/m for Cs and Rb) and from the Penning-trap electron g-factor combined with QED. These AMO inputs dominate the CODATA values of α, R∞ and m_e, and the ~5σ gap between the Cs and Rb values remains unresolved.

name: Optical clocks and redefining the second
summary: Optical lattice and ion clocks now beat the Cs primary standard by about 100×. The CIPM roadmap therefore plans an optical redefinition of the second around 2030, continuing the 2019 move to defining units by fixed constants.

name: No-go theorems as experimental metaphysics
summary: The Bell, Kochen–Specker and PBR theorems turn questions about hidden variables, locality and the reality of the wavefunction into constraints that experiments can test. Philosophy of physics now argues over which premise to give up, such as measurement independence or outcome independence.

name: Dirac notation and operator algebra
summary: The working tools of QM are linear-algebra results: commutators and simultaneous diagonalisation, unitary changes of basis, ladder-operator algebras, and rigged Hilbert spaces for the continuous spectra of position and momentum.

name: Path-integral quantum Monte Carlo and the sign problem
summary: Slicing imaginary time turns the quantum partition function into a classical ensemble of ring polymers that Metropolis sampling can handle. This is exact for bosons, but fermion exchange produces negative weights. That is the sign problem, which is NP-hard in general (Troyer–Wiese 2005).

name: Amplitude estimation speeds up Monte Carlo quadratically
summary: Amplitude amplification estimates an expectation value to error ε with O(1/ε) oracle calls, against O(1/ε²) samples classically (Montanaro 2015). It is the same 1/√N to 1/N jump as from the standard quantum limit to the Heisenberg limit.

name: Tensor-network contraction vs quantum-advantage claims
summary: After the random-circuit-sampling advantage claims (Arute et al. 2019), tensor-network contraction simulated the same circuits classically far faster than first estimated. The treewidth of a circuit's tensor network sets the classical cost, so tensor networks mark the moving boundary of quantum advantage.

name: Neural quantum states and volume-law entanglement
summary: Neural networks such as restricted Boltzmann machines and transformers serve as variational wavefunctions trained by variational Monte Carlo. An MPS's entanglement is capped at ln χ, but these networks can encode volume-law entanglement with polynomially many parameters (Deng, Li & Das Sarma 2017).

name: Born–Oppenheimer surfaces drive ab initio MD
summary: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation separates electrons from nuclei, with small parameter (m_e/M)^{1/4}. Ab initio and Car–Parrinello MD move classical nuclei on the electronic ground-state energy surface. The approximation fails at conical intersections, where nonadiabatic methods such as surface hopping take over.

name: Trotter splitting: symplectic integrators and quantum gates
summary: Leapfrog and Strang symplectic integrators and split-step Schrödinger solvers use the same operator splitting that compiles e^{-iHt} into gates on a quantum computer. Higher-order Suzuki formulas and their commutator error bounds carry over directly.

name: Lippmann–Schwinger equation and the Born series
summary: The outgoing Helmholtz Green's function turns the Schrödinger equation into an integral equation. Iterating it gives the Born series, and its far-field limit gives the scattering amplitude f(θ).
map: \psi=\phi+G_0^{(+)}V\psi,\ G_0^{(+)}(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar^2}\frac{e^{ik|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Analytic S-matrix: poles, resonances, dispersion
summary: Causality makes partial-wave S-matrices analytic in complex momentum. Bound states are poles on the positive imaginary k axis and resonances are poles below the real axis that give Breit–Wigner peaks. The optical theorem and dispersion relations tie forward amplitudes to total cross sections.

name: Saddle points, Stokes lines and instantons
summary: Semiclassics evaluates the path integral by stationary phase or steepest descent. Airy functions join WKB solutions at turning points, Stokes phenomena control tunnelling exponents, and Wick rotation turns tunnelling into Euclidean instanton saddles.
map: \int\mathcal Dx\,e^{iS/\hbar}\approx\sum_{\rm cl}A_{\rm cl}\,e^{iS_{\rm cl}/\hbar},\ t\to-i\tau,\ \Gamma\propto e^{-S_E^{\rm inst}/\hbar}

name: Berry phase as holonomy of a U(1) connection
summary: The Berry connection is a connection on the line bundle of eigenstates over parameter space. Its curvature 2-form integrates to the Berry phase, and over closed surfaces to integer Chern numbers (Simon 1983). The quantum geometric tensor combines the Fubini–Study metric with the Berry curvature.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Schmidt decomposition is the singular value decomposition
summary: Arrange a bipartite pure state's amplitudes as a matrix and its SVD is the Schmidt form. The squared singular values are the eigenvalues of the reduced state, so entanglement entropy and Schmidt rank are matrix invariants. The same SVD truncation drives DMRG.

name: PT symmetry and exceptional points
summary: A non-Hermitian Hamiltonian that commutes with the antiunitary PT operator has a real spectrum while the symmetry is unbroken. At the breaking threshold, eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce at an exceptional point: H becomes a non-diagonalisable Jordan block, the eigenvalues meet at a square-root branch point, and the splitting grows as √ε.
sources: Bender & Boettcher (1998). "Real Spectra in Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians Having P T Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 5243. [doi:10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243)

name: Kramers degeneracy from T² = −1 for half-integer spin
summary: Time reversal is antiunitary and acts on spin as Θ = e^{-iπS_y/ħ}K, so Θ² = (−1)^{2S}. With an odd number of electrons, every level is at least doubly degenerate unless a magnetic field breaks T. This is the origin of the protected Kramers pairs in topological insulators.

name: Atomic parity violation and electron EDM searches
summary: Z-boson exchange mixes S and P states, so the forbidden Cs 6S–7S transition gains a parity-odd amplitude that measures the weak charge Q_W (Wood et al. 1997). Electron-EDM searches in heavy atoms and polar molecules test T, and hence CP, violation; the best bound is |d_e| < 4.1×10^{-30} e·cm (JILA HfF+, 2023).

name: Dyson's threefold way fixes chaotic level statistics
summary: Spectra of chaotic systems follow random-matrix statistics (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit 1984). Antiunitary symmetry picks the ensemble: GOE if T² = +1, GUE if T is broken, GSE if T² = −1. The level-repulsion exponent β is the diagnostic.

name: Hidden SO(4) symmetry of the hydrogen atom
summary: On bound states, the angular momentum L and the scaled Runge–Lenz vector K generate so(4) ≅ su(2)⊕su(2). Pauli (1926) used this to obtain the Bohr levels algebraically, and it explains the n² degeneracy across ℓ. SU(3) plays the same role for the 3D isotropic oscillator.

name: Quantum Noether: conserved generators commute with H
summary: By Wigner's theorem, symmetries act as unitary or antiunitary operators. If a continuous symmetry e^{-iθG/ħ} leaves H invariant, then [G,H] = 0 and the distribution of G is conserved. This is the operator form of Noether's theorem: momentum from translations, J from rotations, charge from U(1).

name: BEC breaks U(1); Bogoliubov phonon is the Goldstone mode
summary: The condensate order parameter ψ = √n e^{iθ} breaks the global phase symmetry that goes with atom-number conservation. The gapless Bogoliubov sound mode is the Goldstone boson, and its sound speed sets the Landau critical velocity for superfluid flow.

name: Time crystals break time-translation symmetry
summary: Wilczek's (2012) equilibrium time crystal is ruled out by the Watanabe–Oshikawa no-go theorem. Instead, periodically driven many-body systems, which conserve quasienergy rather than energy, break the discrete Floquet time-translation symmetry and respond at period 2T. Many-body localization or prethermalization protects this order, which has been seen with trapped ions, NV centres and superconducting qubits.

name: Hydrogen spectroscopy, R∞ and the proton radius
summary: The Rydberg constant and the proton charge radius are fitted together to hydrogen and deuterium transition frequencies. The muonic-hydrogen Lamb shift (2010) gave a radius 4% smaller. The puzzle eased once newer hydrogen measurements and CODATA 2018/2022 moved to about 0.84 fm.

name: Clock ratios test the constancy of α and m_p/m_e
summary: Different transitions depend on α and μ = m_p/m_e with different sensitivities, so repeated ratios between clocks (Al+/Hg+, Yb+ E3/E2, Cs/Sr) bound present-day drifts at the ~10^{-18} per year level. The same ratios search for ultralight dark matter, which would make the constants oscillate.
sources: Rosenband et al. (2008). "Frequency Ratio of Al+and Hg+Single-Ion Optical Clocks; Metrology at the 17th Decimal Place". *Science* 319, 1808. [doi:10.1126/science.1154622](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1154622)

name: Unitary Fermi gas: universality from a missing scale
summary: At a Feshbach resonance the scattering length diverges and drops out, leaving density as the only scale. Dimensional analysis then forces every observable to be a universal number times its free-Fermi-gas value, the Bertsch parameter ξ being one example. Dilute neutron matter shares the same universality.

name: Clock uncertainty budgets and Allan deviation
summary: Clock accuracy is quoted as a GUM-style budget of Type B systematic shifts (blackbody, Zeeman, Stark, motional) added in quadrature. Stability is quoted as the Allan deviation, which quantum projection noise ultimately limits. This is how the Al+/Hg+ ratio reached the 17th decimal place.
sources: Rosenband et al. (2008). "Frequency Ratio of Al+and Hg+Single-Ion Optical Clocks; Metrology at the 17th Decimal Place". *Science* 319, 1808. [doi:10.1126/science.1154622](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1154622)

name: Quantum Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
summary: Optimising the classical Cramér–Rao bound over all quantum measurements gives the quantum Fisher information (Braunstein–Caves 1994). N independent probes give F_Q = N, the standard quantum limit; entangled probes reach up to N², the Heisenberg limit.

name: Cryogenic sensors as single-photon detectors
summary: Cryogenic sensors and the noise analysis of instrumentation have become quantum-optics hardware. Transition-edge sensors resolve photon number with about 95% efficiency, and superconducting nanowire detectors reach about 98% efficiency with few-picosecond jitter. Dark counts and dead time are the other figures of merit.

name: Quantum-limited amplifiers for qubit readout
summary: Dispersive readout of superconducting qubits needs Josephson parametric or travelling-wave amplifiers that work near the Caves bound: a phase-insensitive amplifier must add at least half a quantum of noise. The same SQUID and Josephson technology reads out cryogenic detectors.

name: Typicality and ETH as foundations of statistical mechanics
summary: Philosophy of statistical mechanics asks why equilibrium ensembles work. Canonical typicality (almost every pure state of system plus bath has a thermal reduced state) and ETH (every energy eigenstate looks thermal) answer this for isolated quantum systems without ensembles or the ergodic hypothesis.
